title: Competency credential — what a person demonstrated, and who stood behind it
description: The portable attestation the individual OWNS. It serializes into a W3C Verifiable Credential 2.0 with an Open Badges 3.0 achievement, and this schema governs the claim payload that becomes the credentialSubject. Verification is a signature check against a signed issuer trust registry distributed as a file — no ledger, no network, no call to the issuer. A credential attests competence and NEVER authority: see authorization.schema.json, and decision 6 in CLAUDE.md. Held in dual custody, because ISO/IEC 17025 §6.2 requires the laboratory to hold competence records for audit while the individual needs portability; both hold a true copy and neither can erase the other's.

id.description: Stable identifier for this credential. A UUID rather than a sequence: issuance happens offline and in parallel across organizations that cannot coordinate a counter.

subject.description: The person who holds this. Minimal PII by design — a DID, not a name, birthdate or national ID. A holder may bind a display name locally; nothing requires it to travel.

kind.description: Recorded on the credential itself, not merely resolvable from the taxonomy. A reader years later must be able to tell what KIND of claim this is — explanation, performance, or defended judgement — without the corpus in hand.

assessedAtScope.description: Every level is assessed at element scope, so 'CM-03-048 at L2' means that element was assessed and not that some cluster containing it was. Fixed as a const because a credential's meaning cannot be renegotiated after issue; an overlay making the opposite trade must say so on its own credentials rather than reusing this schema.

expiresOn.description: Recertification date, from the level default unless the element overrides it. An expired credential is not a false one: it remains true that the competence was demonstrated on the date it was demonstrated. Verifiers decide what weight to give currency.

provenanceTier.description:
VISIBLE, always. This is how the entry-barrier principle and the rigor principle coexist: nothing is blocked, and the difference is legible rather than hidden. A hiring manager sees not only what was demonstrated but who stood behind it. Suppressing this field in a renderer defeats the design.

CHECKED, NOT MERELY DECLARED. The validator computes the highest tier this credential's own evidence supports and rejects anything above it. Each step up requires something a reader can verify offline in the document itself: `self-study` needs a signer who is not the subject; `peer-reviewed` needs a signer whose standing is EVIDENCED, by an authority chain or a founding-cohort basis, so an unbacked `heldLevel` or `credentialedReviewer` does not lift the tier; `organization` needs an issuer recorded as a registered entity, with a name and a resolvable trust-registry entry rather than an individual's DID alone; `accredited-body` needs the issuer's own accreditation recorded. Understating is permitted and silent — claiming less than you can prove misleads nobody.

`authority` CANNOT CURRENTLY BE ISSUED. It denotes the neutral-foundation issuer of last resort, which needs funding and legal existence and does not exist. See open decision 4.

WHAT `self-study` MEANS, since reading it against 'no self-signoff, ever' has caused genuine confusion. It describes the STANDING OF THE WITNESS, not their absence. Somebody who is not the subject still signs — a colleague, a mentor, a former supervisor — and that person holds no credential and no reviewer authority, which is why `heldLevel: null` is legitimate at L1 and L2. A person with no employer and no professional network can therefore earn and hold something real, which is the entry-barrier principle working rather than a hole in it.

It is NOT the same statement as 'an unanchored ledger supports self-study claims'. That sentence is about an attempt record. Every credential has a signer and every signoff anchors the ledger, so an unanchored ledger backs no credential at any tier, including this one. See attempt-ledger.schema.json.

assessment.description: How it was earned, recorded so a reader need not assume.

archetypes.description: Which item shapes were served. Archetype IDs are append-only precisely so this stays resolvable after an archetype is retired.

attemptRef.description: Pointer into the attempt ledger. What makes 'one attempt, no retakes' mean anything for a challenge exam.

candidateOrganization.description:
The organization the candidate belonged to at assessment. Recorded ONLY so the cross-organizational signer rule can be evaluated as written — 'at least one signer outside the candidate's own organization'. Without it a verifier can approximate the rule but cannot apply it, and the approximation wrongly rejects a candidate whose two signers both come from a single different organization.

Omit it where the rule does not apply. Deliberately the organization and not the person's role, team or location: minimal PII is a design constraint, and signer organizations already travel on the credential for the same reason.

Carry `id` where one exists. The rule is decided by comparing this against the signers' organizations, and without identifiers that comparison is between strings somebody typed.

activities.description:
THE EXPERIENCE CLAIM ITSELF, rather than a total. Required wherever the level sets `minExperienceHours` above zero — L3 and up — and absent at L1 and L2, which are entry rungs and must not acquire a burden.

This used to be two integers: `experienceHours` and `distinctActivities`. Decision 37 is right that one activity credits every element it genuinely exercises, and the inverse risk is the one those integers could not touch: forty hours claimed against seventeen elements, with nothing recording which part of the work demonstrated which. Seventeen credentials each reading `experienceHours: 40` look identical whether the activity genuinely exercised all seventeen or exercised two and the rest were claimed by association. **A declaration is reviewable evidence only if there is something to review.**

BOTH TOTALS ARE NOW DERIVED FROM THIS AND NEITHER IS DECLARED. Hours are the sum; distinct activities are the count of distinct `id`s. Carrying a separate total alongside the list would be two copies of one fact that drift after an edit, and it is the copy a reader trusts that would be wrong.

EVERY ACTIVITY OWES AN ACCOUNT OR A PINNED RECORD, and `demonstrates` either way. A holder who cannot describe a customer's work pins it instead — see `account`, which used to compel a disclosure that was not always theirs to make.

THE SAME ACTIVITY IS WRITTEN ON EVERY CREDENTIAL IT CREDITS, under the same `id`, because a credential verifies offline and has to stand alone. What differs between them is `demonstrates`, which is the whole point.

id.description:
A stable name for this piece of work, chosen by the holder and meaningful only inside their own record — nothing resolves it and no registry holds it.

It exists so that ONE activity is countable as one. Two entries sharing an `id` are one piece of work written twice, and counting them as two is exactly the inflation a breadth threshold exists to stop; across a wallet, the same `id` carrying different hours or a different account is the same inflation spread over several credentials, where no single document looks wrong.

hours.description: Hours of this activity. Under decision 37 the whole figure credits every element the activity genuinely exercised, so it is not exclusive to this credential and must never be summed across a wallet as though it were.

account.description:
What the work actually was, in enough detail that somebody could disagree with the claim. Not a job title and not a date range — what was measured, against what, and what came out.

REQUIRED UNLESS THE ACTIVITY CARRIES A `ref`, AND THAT IS NOT A LOOPHOLE. It used to be required outright, with a floor of eighty characters, which at L5's five activities compelled somewhere upward of four hundred characters describing real work at a real laboratory — on a document built to be handed to a future employer, often a competitor of the laboratory the work was done for.

THE PROBLEM IS NOT LENGTH, IT IS WHOSE INFORMATION IT IS. A calibration laboratory's customer, method and results are the CUSTOMER'S commercial information. The holder is not always at liberty to describe it, and a schema that compels them either extracts a disclosure that was not theirs to make or extracts a sentence vague enough to be worthless — which is the outcome the floor existed to prevent. `evidence[].sufficiency` is not the counter-example it looks like: that is a REVIEWER'S judgement about an artifact, which is part of the attestation, and this is a description of somebody else's business.

AND NOTHING CAN BE REDACTED LATER. `ecdsa-jcs-2019` canonicalizes the whole document (W3C *Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites 1.0* §3.3), so removing a field breaks the signature. The suite that permits it is `ecdsa-sd-2023` (§3.6), whose base-proof/derived-proof mechanism works over canonical N-Quads — RDF, an `@context`, and the network resolution rule 5 forbids and decision 17 already rejected `ecdsa-rdfc-2019` for. **Selective disclosure is not merely unchosen here; it is unavailable.** So whatever is written on this field travels, to everybody, forever.

WHAT TRAVELS INSTEAD, FOR A HOLDER WHO CANNOT SAY MORE. `ref` pins the underlying record by content hash and `demonstrates` says what the work showed about THIS element — which is written in the corpus's own vocabulary, against an anchor, and describes a competence rather than a customer. That is exactly the arrangement `evidence[]` already uses: the artifact is pinned for whoever can reach it, the argument travels for everybody. The signers judged the work with the record in front of them; a later reader gets the hash and the argument.

Where the holder IS at liberty, write it. A thin claim is a weak claim rather than an invalid one, and an account is worth more to a reviewer than a hash.

demonstrates.description:
WHAT THIS ACTIVITY DEMONSTRATED ABOUT THIS ELEMENT, specifically. The field open decision 19 exists for, and the one that differs between the seventeen credentials one activity may credit.

It cannot prove the activity exercised the element — nothing can, and this does not pretend to. What it does is make somebody say HOW. An activity that genuinely exercised two elements and was claimed against seventeen produces fifteen of these that a reviewer can read and find thin, which is the difference between an unreviewable number and reviewable evidence. The same standing `positionNeutrality` and `knowledgeRefs[].supports` have, and stated in the same words.

Write it against the element's ANCHOR at the level being claimed, not against its title.

ref.description:
Content hash of the underlying record — a job log, a set of certificates, a report. The same arrangement `evidence` uses: the rationale travels on the credential where every reader sees it, and the artifact is pinned for the reader who can reach it.

IT IS ALSO WHAT LETS `account` BE OMITTED, for a holder who cannot describe the work without disclosing a customer's business. An activity must carry one or the other: a piece of work with neither a description nor a pinned record asserts nothing anybody could examine, which is what open decision 19 was about.

scorerCount.description: How many people independently scored this assessment. Recorded because L4 and L5 are `doubleScored` in proficiency.yaml and nothing else on the credential could show it — signer count cannot stand in, since SCORING IS NOT SIGNING. Two signers who scored the work once between them satisfy the signer rule and not this one, and the distinction is the whole reason double scoring is specified separately.

previousLevelAttainedOn.description:
When the holder attained the level below this one. Recorded on the credential rather than left to the issuer's records so that `minDaysSincePreviousLevel` can be checked OFFLINE, by a verifier holding this credential and nothing else — the same reason the experience activities travel here.

The waiting period exists because competence at these levels is partly accumulated practice, which cannot be compressed by sitting assessments faster.

OPEN: direct entry. A candidate who reaches L4 by challenge exam without ever holding L3 has no previous-level date, and what the waiting period means for them is not yet decided. Until it is, the validator requires the date wherever the level sets a period, which is the conservative reading.

definitionRef.description:
REQUIRED. Hash of the element definition as it stood when this credential was issued, projected to the fields that carry meaning for the attested level: kind, levelCeiling, demonstration, and the anchor for that level.

`demonstration` is in the projection because it decides what evidence is ADMISSIBLE for the claim. Without it an element could be flipped from `desk` to `equipment` with the anchor untouched, the hash would still match, and a verifier would read 'definition unchanged' while a credential earned by desk work sat under a definition demanding witnessed work at a bench.

`status`, `roleTargets` and `prerequisites` are excluded on purpose rather than by oversight. Status is checked at issue by the attestable-status rule; pinning it would make an ordinary draft-to-stable promotion, or a deprecation, report drift on every credential already issued. Role targets state what roles need rather than what this person demonstrated, and gap analysis must read today's. Prerequisites are the preparation graph, and somebody who met the anchor met it whatever route was recommended at the time.

Append-only IDs guarantee that 'CM-03-014' always RESOLVES. They do not guarantee it always MEANS the same thing — anchors get rewritten and ceilings get revised, and nothing in an immutable identifier prevents either. Without this pin, the same credential string earned in 2027 and in 2030 could attest materially different competence and a verifier would silently apply the newer meaning.

A hash rather than a version number, because a version number depends on somebody remembering to increment it. Drift is NOT invalidity: a credential whose pin no longer matches remains exactly true of the definition in force when it was earned, and a reader should be shown that definition rather than the current one.

assessmentPolicyRef.description:
REQUIRED. Hash of the assessment policy in force for this level when the credential was issued — the whole level entry from content/competence/taxonomy/proficiency.yaml.

`definitionRef` pins what the ELEMENT meant. This pins what the LEVEL meant, and without both, decision 39 is only half applied. The proficiency ladder controls signer count, the level a witness must hold, whether a credentialed reviewer and a cross-organizational signer are required, double scoring, capstone, work product, mentoring, minimum experience hours, the waiting period and recertification. Its own schema states that changing a level's meaning retroactively changes what every existing credential asserts.

Concretely: if L4 requires 200 hours and two reviewers today and 500 hours and three in three years, an old credential still reads the same and its definitionRef still matches, because the element did not move — the bar did. This field is what lets a reader tell.

It answers the question that actually matters when reading an old credential: not merely 'what did L4 mean' but 'what rules had to be satisfied for this to be issued'.

knowledgeSnapshot.description:
The BOK sections the element pointed at when this was issued, pinned by content. Answers the second half of 'what did this mean at the time' — not only what the person was claimed to be able to do, but what the reference material said. A section rewritten after a standard revision changes what the claim rested on, and a reader assessing an older credential needs to know that.

AT LEAST ONE, mirroring `knowledgeRefs` on the element, which has the same floor. Without it the requirement was shape-only: an empty array satisfied 'pin the knowledge' while pinning none of it, the drift check iterated nothing and reported nothing, and every element carries at least one knowledgeRef to pin. A pin that can be satisfied by pinning nothing is not a pin.

custody.description:
WHO HOLDS A TRUE COPY OF THIS, and under what obligation. Decision 23 said the credential is held in dual custody — the laboratory needs a competence record it can produce at audit under ISO/IEC 17025:2017 §6.2, the individual needs portability — and until now that was a sentence in this description and nothing else. A single object with no record of who else holds it cannot express a two-custodian arrangement, so 'dual custody' was a claim the data could neither carry nor contradict.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT FIX. It does not stop a laboratory purging its copy; nothing in a file held by somebody else can. What it does is make the arrangement legible: a verifier reading the holder's copy after a purge sees that Lab A took custody with a retention obligation running to a stated date, so the absence is a records-management failure somebody can name rather than a silence. That is what a record is for.

It also closes the reverse case, which is the one that harms the holder. An organization could issue a credential ABOUT somebody, retain it, and never deliver it — leaving a person unable to prove a competence that has been formally attested. A `holder` entry whose custodian is the subject is required, so a credential that never reached the person it describes cannot be well-formed.

DIVERGENCE BETWEEN COPIES NEEDS NOTHING FURTHER. Every credential is signed, so two copies that differ in content cannot both verify — the cryptography already answers it, and adding a content hash here would be a second, weaker mechanism for a question the first one settles. What signatures cannot detect is a copy that does not EXIST, and that is precisely what this array records.

Related but distinct: `organization-custody` in attempt-ledger.schema.json anchors the attempt chain as a side effect of the same retention obligation. Different object, same clause.

custodian.description: The DID of a person, or the name of an organization. A `holder` entry MUST carry the subject's own DID; anything else means the entry describes somebody who is not the holder.

role.description: `holder` — the individual whose credential this is. `issuing-organization` — the body that issued it and carries the §6.2 retention obligation. `assessing-organization` — where assessment happened somewhere other than the issuer, which has its own records to keep.

retentionUntil.description: When the custodian's retention obligation ends. Expected on an organization custodian: ISO/IEC 17025:2017 §8.4 requires records to be retained for a DEFINED period, and 'indefinitely, probably' is not a defined period. Absent on a `holder` entry, because the individual owns their copy and owes nobody a retention schedule — that asymmetry is the whole point of the credential being theirs.

retentionBasis.description: Why this custodian retains it — the clause or policy imposing the obligation. Example: ISO/IEC 17025:2017 §8.4.2.

evidence.description:
Archived, hashed artifacts. Hashing is what lets any credential be independently re-reviewed years later — including by someone challenging it.

AND HASHING IS ONLY HALF OF IT. A hash proves an artifact has not changed; it says nothing about why it was ENOUGH. Without `sufficiency` a credential carries `sha256:…` and a date, and the re-reviewer can confirm the artifact is the one submitted while having no way to discover what the reviewer thought it demonstrated. The archive exists for re-review, and re-review needs the original judgement to test.

sufficiency.description:
WHY THIS ARTIFACT WAS ENOUGH — the reviewer's sufficiency decision, recorded where the artifact is.

REQUIRED ON EVERY ARTIFACT SOMEBODY JUDGED: `work-product`, `capstone`, `defense-record` and `mentoring-record`. Deliberately NOT on `attempt`, which is a pointer into the ledger — a record of what happened rather than an artifact a reviewer decided was sufficient. Demanding a rationale there would produce a sentence written to satisfy a validator, which is worse than the silence it replaced.

`decidedBy` MUST BE ONE OF THE SIGNERS, and the validator checks it. A sufficiency judgement by somebody who did not sign is not part of this attestation: it is an opinion attached to a credential, reading as though it carried the weight of the signature beside it.

rationale.description:
What the artifact showed, against the anchor for the attested level. Long enough to be argued with: "meets the L4 anchor" restates the claim and tells a re-reviewer nothing, while "retained the contribution the template drops, showed what it did to the combined figure, and defended the inclusion when pressed on whether it had been chosen to reach a wanted result" can be tested against the artifact.

The counterpart of `cannotConvey` on a module and `lookupResistance` on an archetype: a required sentence that cannot be faked by leaving it vague, because the vagueness is the visible part.

signers.description: Who attested. NO SELF-SIGNOFF EVER: the validator rejects a credential whose subject appears here. Structural, not procedural — a rule enforced only by policy is a rule that fails under pressure.

heldLevel.description: The level this signer held IN THIS ELEMENT at signing time. Null is legitimate at L1 and L2, where a witness attests only that they saw the work.

authority.description:
The signer's own credentials, backing the claims they make about themselves.

WITHOUT THIS, `heldLevel: 4` AND `credentialedReviewer: true` ARE ASSERTIONS. That is the same 'trust me' this system exists to eliminate, reappearing one level up: a credential whose whole purpose is to replace an unevidenced claim about a candidate should not rest on an unevidenced claim about the signer.

WHAT A CHAIN NEEDS IN ORDER TO RESOLVE, stated correctly — this used to end 'Nothing in that requires contacting anybody', and that was wrong. A verifier can establish the chain offline only if they HOLD the backing credential: `credentialId` and `credentialRef` are an identifier and a hash, and a hash is opaque to anybody without the thing it hashes. What is free of the network is the CHECKING; obtaining the document is not, and the two were run together.

AND THE HOLDER'S WALLET CANNOT SUPPLY IT. The obvious repair — export the signers' credentials alongside the holder's — is refused, because a signer's competence record is the SIGNER'S record. Rule 6b is not a rule about one person; conscripting a third party's credential into somebody else's wallet, to be shown to whoever that person shows it to, is the disclosure this project built a whole schema to prevent. A narrower derived proof would need selective disclosure, which `ecdsa-jcs-2019` does not have and `ecdsa-sd-2023` cannot provide here because its mechanism is RDF-based. **So a resolvable chain is something the SIGNER consents to hand over, and it is not something `walletExport` can manufacture.**

WHICH IS WHY THE ENTRY NAMES WHAT IT CLAIMS. `element` and `level` make the claim legible to a verifier who does not hold the backing credential, and FALSIFIABLE to one who later does — the hash pins the document, so a claim that disagrees with it is a detectable lie rather than an unexaminable assertion. Without them the entry told a reader nothing at all, which is worse than telling them something they can check later.

A reader must never take those two fields for a resolved chain. `checkCredential` resolves them when it is handed the backing credentials and says so in either case, on the same argument as `signatureVerified` on a trust verdict: the honest answer is a fact about what the caller had in front of them.

Optional today because there are no credentials yet to reference, and a founding-cohort signer legitimately holds none. The validator warns whenever a claim is unbacked. It becomes mandatory when the credential engine can resolve chains — see Phase 6.

basis.description: `held-level` backs the signer's competence in this element. `reviewer-authority` backs their standing to review at all — a separate competence covering review methodology, rubric calibration and bias.

element.description:
The element the backing credential attests. For `held-level` this is normally the element being signed off — the signoff policy asks for competence IN THE SAME ELEMENT — and for `reviewer-authority` it is a different element entirely, covering review methodology, rubric calibration and bias.

It is a CLAIM about a document the reader may not hold, and it is checked against that document the moment they do.

level.description: The level the backing credential attests. What the signoff policy's `witnessMustHoldLevel` is actually compared against once the chain resolves — and, until then, what a reader is told is being claimed rather than left to infer from an identifier.

bootstrapAuthority.description:
Present when this signer signed under FOUNDING-COHORT authority rather than by holding the level themselves.

The ladder cannot start on its own: L3 requires an L4 signer, L4 requires L5, and L5 requires L5, so with no holders only L1 and L2 are reachable. A closed, time-limited founding cohort admitted on demonstrated external standing breaks the deadlock.

IT MUST NEVER BE INVISIBLE. A bootstrap-signed L5 is not a peer-signed L5, and a reader who cannot tell them apart has been misled about the strongest claim the system makes. The marker is permanent — it is not cleared when the cohort closes, because the credential was still signed that way.

basis.description: The external standing this signer was admitted on — a primary-laboratory or NMI appointment, accreditation assessor status, a publication record. Stated per signer rather than assumed from cohort membership, so a reader can weigh it rather than take it on trust.

organization.description: Recorded so cross-organizational signing at L5 is checkable, and so reciprocal-review patterns can be detected. Supply `id` where the organization has one — an L5 credential whose cross-organizational rule was decided by comparing two typed strings is carrying a weaker guarantee than it appears to, and the validator will say so.

name.description: The issuing entity's name. Together with `trustRegistryEntry` this is what distinguishes an ORGANIZATION standing behind a credential from an individual who happened to sign it, which is the step from the `peer-reviewed` tier to `organization`.

trustRegistryEntry.description: Key into the signed issuer trust registry. Verification resolves the issuer here, offline, from a distributed file — never by contacting the issuer.

accreditationRecognition.description:
The issuer's OWN accreditation, as the recognizing body records it — a schedule of accreditation and its number, or an equivalent identifier. Required for the `accredited-body` provenance tier, which cannot otherwise be distinguished from `organization` by anything a reader can check.

This is the issuer's accreditation, NOT the holder's authorization to work under it. Those are different objects and the difference is load-bearing: see authorization.schema.json, whose `grantedBy.accreditationRecognition` records the same fact about a grant that ends when the person leaves. A credential is portable and an authorization is not, so this field says who stood behind the assessment and never what the holder may do.

portable.description: Competency credentials travel with the person. Stated explicitly and redundantly so that the contrast with an authorization is visible in the data itself, not only in documentation — see authorization.schema.json, where the same field is const false.

status.description: Revocation exists for fraud and for demonstrable assessment failure. It does NOT exist for an employer who has fallen out with the holder: a competency credential records something that happened, and an organization cannot un-happen it.

proof.description:
Signed by the ISSUER. A credential is the whole product of this system — the thing a person owns and carries to somebody who has never met them — and unsigned it is a text file asserting its own truth.

It is required. It was not, and a credential carrying no proof at all was schema-valid, passed every check in `credentials.ts` without a finding, and returned a populated verdict from `verifyAgainstRegistry`.

did.description: A decentralized identifier. The method is deliberately not fixed here — the Personal edition must work with no server and no registrar, so a purely cryptographic method has to remain viable.
